summary:
For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we selected the Mission Design Game challenge to transform NASA’s dense onboarding, orientation, and technical training materials into an accessible, interactive learning experience. Instead of passively reading complex manuals, players learn real aerospace engineering principles and mission protocols by actively playing through authentic space scenarios.
In the game, players are presented with three specific mission problems such as repairing the International Space Station, remotely commanding Mars rovers with signal delays, and installing a Lunar Fission Surface Power system must design and execute the right space mission architecture to solve them. By gamifying real NASA mission data our project makes space mission training engaging, intuitive, and effective for new recruits, students, and space enthusiasts alike.
details:
Our project is an interactive, educational mission-design simulation game built to modernize NASA’s onboarding, orientation, and technical training workflows for designing missions. Players step into the role of a mission engineer and progress through four authentic, data-driven space scenarios. In the ISS mission, players simulate rocket launch parameters and restore orbital communications on the International Space Station. In the Mars mission, they command their chosen rover across three real sampling sites—Crater Floor/Rochette (Montdenier), Delta Front/Wildcat Ridge (Hazeltop), and Neretva Vallis/Cheyava Falls (Sapphire Canyon). Throughout this stage, players must account for Earth–Mars signal delays, unlocking real NASA terrain photography and science briefs as they go. Next, in the Moon mission, players assemble a planned 2030 Lunar Fission Surface Power reactor or a solar panel array to solve continuous lunar energy requirements. Finally, in the collaboration mission, three players work together to complete all scenarios, with the fastest player earning extra credits.

Traditional aerospace onboarding and technical training rely heavily on dense manuals and lengthy reports. Our solution embeds verified NASA mission protocols, telemetry constraints, and real geological data directly into hands-on gameplay. This lowers the barrier to entry for new recruits, trainees, and students. It also helps them build systems-thinking, mission-planning, and real-time crisis communication skills in an engaging, active format. Rather than creating a generic arcade space game, we focused on integrating game-based learning into highly specialized, infrastructure- and knowledge-intensive domains like NASA’s planetary exploration programs. The result is a functional demo grounded in real engineering constraints, scientific accuracy, active decision-making, and accessibility for learners without a prior aerospace background.

To develop the project, our team built the game using JavaScript, CSS, and HTML. We illustrated our original guide character and designed the user interface and visual assets with Canva. We also integrated official mission archives and imagery from the NASA Mars 2020 Perseverance Sample Catalog, NASA Artemis Fission Surface Power documentation, and NASA ISS resources, alongside educational game mechanics inspired by the Canadian Space Agency (CSA) and Picnic Platform
